Driving and delivery jobs cover a wide spectrum — from flexible local delivery and courier work you can do part-time, to full-time CDL truck driving that pays well and is in steady demand. Requirements vary a lot by role: local delivery usually needs a standard license and clean record, while commercial trucking requires a CDL. Some roles provide the vehicle, while gig-style delivery uses your own car. Because goods move everywhere, driving openings tend to be available in most areas year-round. Here's how the roles compare and where to find current openings.

Types of driving jobs

  • Local delivery driver (van / car)
  • Courier and same-day delivery
  • CDL truck driver — regional and long-haul
  • Non-CDL box truck driver
  • Rideshare and on-demand (flexible hours)

What the work is really like day-to-day

The daily routine depends heavily on the role. Local delivery and courier drivers make many stops per shift, so the day is a mix of driving and getting in and out to hand off packages, which involves some lifting. Box-truck drivers handle larger loads and often help load and unload. CDL drivers spend long stretches on the road on regional or long-haul routes, following hours-of-service rules and managing their time carefully. Rideshare and on-demand work lets you choose when to drive, with earnings tied to how much you take on.

Requirements to know

  • Most local delivery: valid license + clean driving record
  • CDL roles: commercial license (some employers help you train)
  • Age and background requirements vary by employer
  • Some roles provide the vehicle; others use your own

Schedules and shifts

Driving covers everything from fixed full-time routes to fully flexible gig work.

  • Full-time regional and local routes
  • Part-time and weekend delivery shifts
  • Flexible, choose-your-own-hours gig delivery
  • Long-haul roles can mean days away from home

Pay range

Flexible and local delivery roles sit at the lower-to-middle of the range above; CDL and specialized trucking roles pay the most, sometimes well beyond it for experienced long-haul drivers. Confirm pay, mileage, and bonuses on each posting.

Common questions

Do I need a CDL to drive for delivery?

No — most local delivery, courier, and box-truck roles use a standard driver's license. A CDL is required for larger commercial trucks, and some employers help you train for one.

Are there flexible driving jobs?

Yes. Delivery, courier, and on-demand roles often let you choose part-time or flexible hours.

Which driving jobs pay the most?

Experienced CDL and long-haul trucking roles generally pay the most, followed by specialized box-truck and regional routes.

What do employers check before hiring?

Most driving roles require a valid license and a review of your driving record, plus a background check. CDL roles have additional requirements, and some include a road test or drug screening. Each posting lists the specifics.

Can I use my own car?

For gig-style and some courier roles, yes — you drive your own vehicle. Many local-delivery and box-truck roles provide a company vehicle instead. The posting will say which applies.
